metaDescription: Six lightweight folding canes compared by weight, folded length, height range and lock design, so you can pick one that packs small and fits your height.
introParagraphs: A folding cane earns its place by disappearing into a purse, glove box or carry-on, then locking into a rigid shaft when you need it. The word lightweight sounds simple, but it hides real tradeoffs: thinner tubing saves ounces yet may flex, and more fold sections mean a smaller package with more joints to inspect.

This lineup covers six aluminum folding canes from Vive, COMFKEY, Vaunn Medical, supregear, CLOKTA and PELEGON. They differ in height span, number of sections, lock style and what is stated on the product page, and those differences decide which one suits a short walker, a tall walker or someone who mostly travels.

We evaluated them from the listings and published specs, not from hands-on use. Treat every height range and capacity as something to confirm on the product page and on the cane itself, and ask a physical therapist if you are unsure how a cane should be fitted.

products.name: supregear Folding Cane, 5-Level Adjustable
products.description:
The supregear cane is the lightest pick here on paper, at about half a pound, and it folds into four sections to roughly 10 inches. Anodized aluminum keeps the shaft light, and the five height settings between 33 and 37 inches let you step the length up or down without tools.

The tradeoff is range. A 33 inch minimum is too long for many shorter walkers, and four sections mean four joints that deserve a quick wiggle test every time you open it. A single tip also asks for more balance than a quad base would.

In daily ownership it is the one to slip into a handbag, since it is shorter folded than the PELEGON at 10.5 inches and far lighter than anything with a seat. If you are taller than average and want the simplest possible carry, this is the sensible default, and the included wrist strap keeps it from hitting the floor when you reach for a door.
products.bestFor: Taller walkers who want the lightest, most compact cane for purses and carry-on bags.
pros: Weighs about half a pound for easy carrying
Folds to roughly 10 inches in four sections
Five height settings from 33 to 37 inches
Wrist strap included in the kit
cons: Four joints mean more spots to check

products.name: CLOKTA Folding Cane, 5-Level Adjustable
products.description:
CLOKTA folds to 10.24 inches, which puts it in the same pocket-friendly class as the supregear at about 10 inches. The shaft is corrosion-resistant anodized aluminum, and the listing describes a shaped grip that contours to the hand along with a wrist strap.

What the page leaves out matters. It does not state a weight capacity, and it does not spell out a height span the way the COMFKEY or PELEGON pages do. Five height steps are also coarser than the eight steps some canes offer, so you may land between two settings.

Because the listing is thin on numbers, this pick suits buyers who care mostly about size and are willing to confirm the height range and rating with the seller before ordering. Next to the Vaunn, which adds a pouch and a self-locking joint, the CLOKTA is the simpler, plainer package.
products.bestFor: Buyers who prioritize a very short folded length and will confirm capacity with the seller.
pros: Folds to 10.24 inches for purses and cars
Five adjustable height settings
Corrosion-resistant anodized aluminum shaft
Shaped grip and wrist strap included
cons: Single tip with no standing support
Five steps are coarser than eight
Capacity is not stated in the listing

products.name: PELEGON Folding Cane, 32 to 37 Inch
products.description:
PELEGON gives the lowest minimum height in the group at 32 inches, one inch under the supregear and COMFKEY, with a top of 37 inches. It folds to about 10.5 by 5.1 by 1 inches, so it stays flat in a bag, drawer or car door pocket.

Height is set with a push button and a twist lock, a two-step adjustment that is more secure than a single pin but takes longer when two people share the cane. The listing does not state a weight capacity, so that is a number to verify.

Compared with the COMFKEY at 33 to 37 inches, the PELEGON covers one extra inch for shorter users while keeping a similar maximum. If your fit sits near the bottom of the range, that single inch can be the difference between a comfortable elbow bend and a cane that is simply too long.
products.bestFor: Average and slightly shorter adults who need a 32 inch minimum without losing portability.
pros: Folds to 10.5 by 5.1 by about 1 inches
Push-button plus twist lock for adjustment
Anti-slip tip for everyday surfaces
32 to 37 inch height covers many users
cons: Narrower upper range than a 38 inch cane
Capacity is not stated in the listing

products.name: Vaunn Medical Height Adjustable Folding Cane
products.description:
The Vaunn Medical cane leans on a self-locking joint that fixes the shaft in place when you open it, plus a palm-shaped non-slip handle intended to spread pressure away from the wrist. A wrist strap and a pouch come in the box, which the other canes here mostly do not offer.

The listing does not detail the height range, and it describes a single tip, so you will need to confirm the span against your own measurement before buying. That makes it a slightly riskier choice for anyone at the extremes of height.

The pouch is the practical difference. Where the supregear and CLOKTA rely on a strap alone, the Vaunn gives you a place to store the folded sections so they do not rattle around a bag. If you value an accessory you will actually use on every trip, it is worth the extra verification step.
products.bestFor: Travelers who want a self-locking joint and a pouch included in the box.
pros: Self-locking joint fixes in place when opened
Palm-shaped handle eases wrist pressure
Wrist strap and carry pouch are included
Anodized aluminum keeps weight modest
cons: Height range is not detailed in the listing
Single tip needs more balance than a quad

products.name: Vive Folding Cane, Anodized Aluminum
products.description:
Vive describes a collapsible cane that locks securely once extended, built from corrosion-resistant anodized aluminum. A contoured grip and wrist strap round out the package, and the page frames the grip as a way to reduce hand fatigue, which is a design intent rather than a guarantee.

The weak point is specifics. The listing does not state a folded length or a height span in the copy we reviewed, so it is hard to compare numerically against the supregear at about 10 inches or the PELEGON at 32 to 37 inches. Check the product page for current dimensions before buying.

Its appeal is brand familiarity and a straightforward feature set. If you already own other Vive products or prefer a name you recognize, it is a reasonable choice, though the numbers-first buyer will find more to work with on the COMFKEY or supregear pages.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a familiar brand and a simple locking aluminum cane with a contoured grip.
pros: Corrosion-resistant anodized aluminum frame
Contoured grip aims to cut hand fatigue
Locks in place once the cane is extended
Wrist strap for hands-free moments
cons: Height span is not shown in the listing
Folded size is not given in the listing

products.name: COMFKEY Folding Walking Stick, 33 to 37 Inch
products.description:
COMFKEY folds in five snap sections, the most of any cane here, and adjusts from 33 to 37 inches. The aluminum shaft and rubber base are aimed at outdoor surfaces, and the listing mentions camping and hiking use alongside luggage and backpacks.

Five sections pack small but add joints. Each snap connection is another place to confirm that the cord and pieces are fully seated, and the 33 inch minimum is too long for shorter users. The page does not give a weight capacity, so verify that number.

Of the six, this reads as the most trail-oriented. Where the Vaunn offers a pouch and a self-locking joint for city trips, the COMFKEY gives a hand strap and a rubber base for gravel and grass, making it the one to consider if your walks leave pavement.
products.bestFor: Taller users who walk on mixed outdoor surfaces and want a very small packed size.
pros: Five snap sections pack down small
Non-slip rubber base for outdoor surfaces
Hand strap lets you hang it when folded
Range of 33 to 37 inches for taller users
cons: Five sections mean more joints to check
33 inch minimum is too long for shorter users

buyingCriteria.explanation: A cane that is too long or short changes how your arm and shoulder load. A common way to size it is to stand in your usual shoes with your arm relaxed and set the handle near the wrist crease, leaving a slight bend at the elbow. The PELEGON starts at 32 inches, while the supregear and COMFKEY start at 33 and the Vive and Vaunn pages do not state a range. If your measurement falls under 33 inches, the PELEGON is the only pick here with a published number that covers you.

Lightweight is only useful if you can verify it. Among the six, the supregear is the only listing that states a weight, at about 0.5 lb. Hold any cane at arm's length for a minute before deciding, because a swing weight that feels fine in the hand may tire the wrist on longer walks. If a page gives no weight, treat that as unknown rather than light.

More sections mean a shorter packed size but more joints that can loosen. The COMFKEY uses five sections and the supregear uses four, while the CLOKTA and PELEGON pages emphasize folded lengths of 10.24 and 10.5 inches. A good rule is to choose the fewest sections that still fit your bag, then check every joint each time you open the cane.

The lock is the part that keeps the shaft rigid under load. The Vaunn advertises a self-locking joint, and the PELEGON adds a push button and a twist lock for height. Push buttons are simple but can loosen over time, so watch for any wobble when extended. If the cane ever flexes or clicks under pressure, stop using it and replace it.

A cane should be rated above the user's weight, and the number on the product itself matters more than the listing. None of the CLOKTA, PELEGON or Vaunn pages states a capacity in the copy we reviewed. Ask the seller or check the packaging before you rely on a cane for support. Heavier users should look at models that print a capacity clearly, and a quad option may suit better.

Grip shape affects comfort over long outings. The Vaunn offers a palm-shaped handle, the Vive and CLOKTA describe contoured grips, and every pick includes a strap of some kind. A strap helps when you need both hands at a door, but it should never be wrapped around the wrist in a way you cannot slip out of quickly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Published weight and fold size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated weights and folded dimensions, because lightweight is the entire point of this category. The supregear states about 0.5 lb and 10 inches, the CLOKTA states 10.24 inches, and the PELEGON states 10.5 by 5.1 by about 1 inches. Listings that gave no number were scored on what they did say.

howWeEvaluated.title: Height coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at the stated minimum and maximum height, since a shaft that does not reach your fit cannot be used safely. The PELEGON covers 32 to 37 inches, while the supregear and COMFKEY cover 33 to 37. Picks with no published range lost points for uncertainty.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lock and joint design
howWeEvaluated.description: We read how each cane locks open and adjusts. The Vaunn self-locking joint, the PELEGON push-button and twist lock, and the five-section COMFKEY snap design each have different upkeep needs. More joints scored lower on simplicity but higher on packability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Comfort features
howWeEvaluated.description: Grip shape, straps and extras were weighed. The Vaunn adds a pouch, the Vive and CLOKTA list contoured grips, and the COMFKEY adds a rubber base for outdoor ground. We did not assume comfort claims reduce fatigue for every hand.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The supregear leads on stated weight, the PELEGON on lowest height, the CLOKTA on a short fold, and the COMFKEY on section count. Because several pages omit capacity, no single cane is the clear safe choice for every user, so we ranked on the strength of what each listing proves.

faq.q: Which lightweight folding cane is lightest?
faq.a: Only the supregear lists a weight, at about 0.5 lb. The other pages do not state one, so they cannot be compared fairly. If weight matters to you, hold the cane or ask the seller before buying.

faq.q: How do I know what height to set it to?
faq.a: Stand in your usual shoes with your arm relaxed and set the handle near your wrist crease. A slight bend at the elbow when gripping is the usual guide. A physical therapist can check your fit in person.

faq.q: Are folding canes as stable as fixed canes?
faq.a: A folding cane has joints, so it relies on the lock staying engaged. Buyers should inspect every joint each time and replace a cane that wobbles. A fixed cane has fewer moving parts to monitor.

faq.q: Do any of these have a weight capacity listed?
faq.a: In the copy we reviewed, the CLOKTA, PELEGON and Vaunn pages do not state one. Check the packaging or ask the maker. Do not assume a capacity from the cane's looks.
Not worse, just different. Five sections like the COMFKEY pack smaller but add joints to check. Four like the supregear are a reasonable middle.

faq.q: Will a lightweight cane prevent falls?
faq.a: We cannot make that claim, and no cane guarantees it. A cane is designed to offer extra support while walking, and individual results vary. A professional can advise whether a cane is right for you.

faq.q: Can I use a folding cane outdoors?
faq.a: Many are designed for it, and the COMFKEY lists a rubber base for outdoor surfaces. Wet leaves, ice and gravel change grip, so check the tip often. Replace worn tips promptly.
